newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian commodity auction changes move closer.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian commodity auction changes move closer.

text.p: Ivory Coast is closer to agreeing new rules for its commodity auctions after meeting donors in June, with changes possible by the 1997/98 (Oct-Sept) cocoa and coffee season, donor sources said on Tuesday.

"There have now been some compromises and donors are waiting for Ivory Coast to come back with some specific measures by the next season," said one source close to private talks held since auction were introduced in May 1996. "The donors would like to see the crop sold off under a different arrangement."
Auctions replaced telephone trading in a bid to raise coocoa and coffee market transparency and meet conditions for a $150 million World Bank agriculture loan dating back to 1995.
Exporters have complained that the rules encourage exporters to overbid to win export contracts, with winning prices sometimes above international market rates.
Exporters have also not been penalised for price speculation by shipping later than planned contract months, donors say.

"The government has now released auction trading data to the World Bank from May 1996 (when the auction opened) to March 1997," said one donor source. The data also detailed delays to shipments, plus sales volumes, dates and distribution between bidders, he added. Requests for the data had previously been declined.
Sources say World Bank analysts studying trading data reject claims of overbidding and put late shipments at only about 20 percent of the total.

"The (domestic against world price) difference is linked to the weakness of the French franc against sterling," one industry analyst told Reuters. "Traders buy in CFA francs (which are pegged to the French franc) and sell in pounds (on London's cocoa market). Some exporters are left with currency profits and re-enter the market with more CFA."
Donor sources say Ivorian and London cocoa market price trends since May 1996 show a close correlation, meaning the auction is effective.

"Some exporters and traders are simply in a stronger position than others," one said, citing different variable and fixed costs which allowed some companies to pay higher prices and make up losses down the marketing chain. "That is just a reality of free markets," he added.
Exporters want a role in managing the auction. Under one proposal, their GEPEX trade body would be a co-manager with the Caistab marketing board which currently runs the system.

Donors are awaiting concrete proposals on how that would work. In the meantime, they have compromised on their objection to the introduction of a series of different auction prices aimed at awarding contracts to more bidders in each daily trade session.

"The government has said it would accept three levels of prices at which contracts would be awarded," one exporter told Reuters this week. "The World Bank has agreed on condition that opening and closing prices on the auction are published," in order to raise market transparency and send signals to producers.
Exporters had originally asked for an auction with five different price levels.

Under current auction rules, a highest bidder wins but pays the price bid by the second highest bidder, who may also win contracts if enough are on offer in a particular session. Volumes for sale are not published before trading.
Donors want rule changes to make exporters pay the price they actually bid for contracts.
"The system depends on traders not knowing how much cocoa is on offer each day. But that is not the case," said one donor. Some had ways of finding out, he added.

In future, Ivorian exporters could also be allowed to buy 100 percent of contracts on offer, sources said. Under the current rules, 15 percent is reserved for direct sale by the Caistab marketing board to foreign traders.
"The 85 to 15 rule could change to say 90 to 10 but in practice there could be no upper ceiling. Local exporters could take 100 percent," said one source.
Donors want Ivory Coast to eliminate forward coffee sales by October 1, 1998, and forward cocoa sales by October 1, 1999.
-- Abidjan newsroom, + 225 21 90 90
